row.name: Tel Hermal Fort
row.description: Tel Hermal (ancient Shaduppum) is an Old Babylonian site in present-day Baghdad, located 600 meters from Tell Muhammad [1]. It was part of the kingdom of Eshnunna, situated on the left bank of the Diyala River near other ancient cities including Eshnunna, Tell Ishchali, and Khafajah [1]. The site yielded important cuneiform archives documenting the kingdom's administration [1]. Its tutelary deity was Bēl-gašer, while the goddess Ninkarrak maintained a cult center at Shaduppum [1].

row.name: Bridge Street Number 39, Chester
row.description: 39 Bridge Street is a Grade I listed building in Chester, England, remarkable for preserving a Roman hypocaust in its cellar dating to the 2nd century AD. The heating system consists of 27 surviving square pillar columns (originally 32 in eight rows) and formed part of the legionary bathhouse serving the Twentieth Legion. Discovered during reconstruction in 1864, the hypocaust is one of the best-preserved in situ Roman remains in Chester. Above ground, the four-storey building incorporates a medieval undercroft from the late 13th or 14th century and a section of the distinctive Chester Rows at first-floor level.

row.name: Ancient Amathunta
row.description: Ancient Amathus was one of the ancient royal cities of Cyprus, thriving from the Archaic period until its decline around 300 BC. Located on the southern coast near modern Agios Tychonas, about 6 miles east of Limassol and 24 miles west of Larnaca, the settlement dates back to the Late Bronze Age (3000–1500 BC). The site features a significant sanctuary dedicated to Aphrodite, considered the second most important cult center in Cyprus after Paphos, reflecting the island's role as the goddess's legendary birthplace.

row.name: Amathus
row.description: Amathus or Amathous was an ancient city-kingdom of Cyprus [1]. Remains of Amathus can be seen today on the southern coast near Agios Tychonas, about 6 miles east of Limassol and 24 miles west of Larnaca [1]. Amathus was built on coastal cliffs with a natural harbour and flourished at an early date, soon requiring several cemeteries [1]. Greeks from Euboea left their pottery at Amathus from the 10th century BC [1]. In the Roman era Amathus became the capital of one of the four administrative regions of Cyprus [1]. Amathus declined and was already almost deserted when Richard Plantagenet took Cyprus in 1191 [1]. From April to May 1930 the Swedish Cyprus Expedition excavated a necropolis on both sides of Amathus's acropolis [1]. In the 1870s, Luigi Palma di Cesnola excavated the necropolis of Amathus, as elsewhere in Cyprus, enriching the early collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art; some objects went to the British Museum [1].

row.name: Banias
row.description: Banias, also spelled Banyas, is a site in the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights, Syria near a natural spring, once associated with the Greek god Pan [1]. The spring is the source of the Banias River, one of the main tributaries of the Jordan River [1]. The spring at Banias initially originated in a large cave carved out of a sheer cliff face which was gradually lined with a series of shrines [1]. The pre-Hellenistic deity associated with the spring of Banias was variously called Ba'al-gad or Ba'al Hermon [1]. Shams al-Mulk Isma'il attacked Banias and captured it on 11 December 1132 [1]. In late spring 1140, Mu'in ad-Din Unur handed Banias to the Crusaders during the reign of King Fulk, due to their assistance against Zengi's aggression towards Damascus [1]. On 18 May 1157, Nūr ad-Din began a siege on Banias using mangonels, a type of siege engine [1].

row.name: Caesarea Philippi
row.description: Caesarea Philippi, originally called Banias, is an ancient site at the foot of Mount Hermon in the Golan Heights. The spring is the source of the Banias River, one of the main tributaries of the Jordan River [1]. Archaeologists uncovered a shrine dedicated to Pan and related deities, and the remains of an ancient city dating from the Hellenistic and Roman periods [1][2]. The city was renamed Caesarea Philippi by Herod's son Philipus to distinguish it from other cities named Caesarea, such as Caesarea Maritima [3].

row.name: Conjunto Arqueologico de Ñustahispana
row.description: Nusta Hispana, also known as Chuquipalta, is an Inca archaeological site near Vilcabamba in Peru's Cusco region, believed to have been the last refuge of the Inca rulers fleeing the Spanish conquest. Its most remarkable feature is Yurac Rumi (White Rock), a massive carved stone outcrop with flat surfaces, stepped sections, and square protrusions. The rock was considered deeply sacred by the Inca, and Augustinian monks later burned the adjacent Temple of the Sun and scorched the rock itself in an act of religious suppression. Hiram Bingham III rediscovered the site on 9 August 1911.

row.name: Ñusta Hispana
row.description: Nusta Hispana (also called Chuquipalta) is an Inca archaeological site in the Vilcabamba region, Cusco, Peru, discovered by Hiram Bingham III on August 9, 1911. Its most notable feature is Yurac Rumi ("White Rock" in Quechua), a carved ceremonial stone with seats and platforms adjacent to a sacred spring. During Titu Cusi's reign, Augustinian friars Marcos and Diego burned down the adjacent Temple of the Sun and scorched the rock, reflecting colonial suppression of indigenous sacred sites. Excavations have yielded 38 pre-Hispanic metal artifacts.

row.name: Thirty-nine (39) Bridge Street, Chester
row.description: A Grade I listed building in Chester, England, notable for the remains of a 2nd-century Roman hypocaust in its cellar, discovered during reconstruction of the property in 1864. The heating system consists of 27 square columns in a chamber that originally held 32 columns in eight rows of four, and was part of the legionary baths complex used by soldiers of the Twentieth Legion. In the late 13th or early 14th century, a medieval undercroft was built adjacent to the hypocaust. Today the ground floor operates as a cafe with cellar access for visitors.

row.name: Shaduppum
row.description: Shaduppum (modern Tell Harmal) was an administrative center in the kingdom of Eshnunna, located in the Diyala River basin near Baghdad, Iraq. Its name means 'the accountant's office' in Akkadian, reflecting its bureaucratic function. Excavated by Iraqi archaeologist Taha Baqir from 1945 to 1963, the site yielded nearly 3,000 cuneiform clay tablets including fragments of the Epic of Gilgamesh, the Laws of Eshnunna predating Hammurabi's Code, and mathematical tablets containing geometric problems resembling Euclidean geometry. The fortified site featured seven temples, including one dedicated to Nisaba, goddess of writing, guarded by terracotta lions dating to 2004-1595 BC.
